content: The 'Scared Straight' program and similar initiatives involve structured visits to prisons by juvenile delinquents or at-risk youth. These programs aim to deter participants from engaging in future criminal behavior by exposing them to the realities of prison life and facilitating interactions with adult inmates. Despite their continued use, research has raised significant doubts about their effectiveness. The objective of this review was to evaluate the impact of these programs on preventing delinquency among juveniles who have been officially adjudicated (convicted by a juvenile court) or pre-delinquents (youths in trouble but not formally convicted). The review sought to determine whether such interventions reduce criminal behavior compared to no intervention. To update the review, a comprehensive search was conducted across 22 electronic databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, and Criminal Justice Abstracts, in December 2011. Additional efforts included consulting experts, searching clinical trial registries, using Google Scholar, and reviewing relevant citations. Studies were included if they involved organized prison visits for juveniles or at-risk youth, used random or quasi-random assignment of participants, included a no-treatment control group, and measured post-visit criminal behavior. The initial search yielded 487 citations, of which 30 were identified as evaluation reports. After further screening, 11 studies were considered potential randomized trials. Upon full-text review, two studies were excluded, leaving nine randomized trials for analysis. Data from these studies were extracted using a standardized tool, and missing outcome data were sought from the original investigators. A second reviewer independently verified the extracted data. The nine included studies were conducted in eight U.S. states between 1967 and 1992, involving nearly 1,000 participants, predominantly male, with an average age of 15 to 17 years. Meta-analyses of seven studies revealed that the intervention was more harmful than no intervention. The odds ratio (OR) for the first post-treatment effect on officially recorded criminal behavior indicated a negative impact of the program (fixed-effect OR 1.68, 95% CI 1.20 to 2.36; random-effects OR 1.72, 95% CI 1.13 to 2.62). Sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of these findings, even when excluding studies with inadequate randomization or high attrition rates. The authors concluded that programs like 'Scared Straight' increase delinquency compared to doing nothing for similar youth populations. Based on these findings, such programs cannot be recommended as effective crime prevention strategies. Agencies that implement these programs must rigorously evaluate their outcomes to ensure they do not inadvertently cause harm to the individuals they aim to help.
